opus-5.5.text:
Well, the core issue is that a benchmark only measures output behavior. It tells you the system produces the right answers on some set of inputs. It tells you almost nothing about *how* it's producing those answers internally. Two systems can have identical performance and completely different internal organization.

This came into focus for me through some work we did comparing networks that were evolved in Picbreeder with networks trained through conventional SGD to produce the exact same images. Same output, pixel for pixel. But when you look inside, it's like night and day. The Picbreeder networks have what we started calling a "unified factored representation." There are clean, modular pieces. You'll find one part of the network that controls, say, the mouth of a skull opening and closing, or symmetry that's captured in a single place and then reused. It's almost like the network discovered the actual underlying regularities of the thing it's depicting.

The SGD networks produce the same picture, but internally it's what we called "fractured entangled representation." Things that should be one concept are split into many disconnected pieces. Things that should be separate are tangled together. It's a kind of imposter intelligence: it looks right from the outside, but the structure underneath is a mess.

Why does that matter if the output is the same? Because the output being the same is only true *on the benchmark*. The representation determines what happens next: how the system generalizes, how it handles novel situations, how it can be built upon, and especially how creative it can be. If you perturb a well-factored representation, you get meaningful variations, like the skull's jaw opening. If you perturb a fractured one, you get garbage. So the representation is really the thing that governs future potential, and the benchmark is completely blind to that.

And I think this connects to a broader theme I've talked about for a long time, which is the danger of objectives. When you optimize hard toward a fixed target, you can get there, but often through a path that produces a deceptive, brittle kind of solution. The Picbreeder networks weren't trying to make a skull. People found the skull serendipitously, stepping through things that were interesting along the way, and that open-ended path seems to have produced much better-organized structure as a byproduct.

So with large models today, when people see high scores and conclude "we're nearly there," my worry is that we may be looking at enormously capable systems with deeply fractured internals. That might show up as weird failures, an inability to do genuinely novel creative work, or a need for ever more data to patch the gaps. The benchmark can't tell you whether you've got a beautiful underlying understanding or a giant pile of entangled heuristics that happens to get the answers right. And those two things have very different futures.

r001.rationale: The response says systems can achieve identical benchmark outputs while having very different internal organization, and describes the SGD representation as fractured and entangled.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing is, a benchmark only measures behavior. It measures the output. And the output can be correct for very different reasons. You can have two networks that get exactly the same score on a benchmark, and one of them has a representation that's beautifully organized, modular, decomposed into the actual regularities of the problem, and the other one is this tangled mess that happens to produce the same answers. From the outside they look identical. But they are not identical, and the difference matters enormously the moment you try to do anything with them beyond that benchmark.

This came out of the work we did on fractured entangled representation, where we looked inside networks that were producing the same images, essentially the same output, but had been arrived at through very different processes. One set came from conventional SGD, and the other came from an open-ended search process, like Picbreeder. And when you look at the internals, the SGD networks are a disaster. The representation is fractured, the same concept is spread across many different pieces that don't talk to each other, and things that should be separate are entangled together. Whereas the Picbreeder-derived networks have this clean, almost human-interpretable decomposition. You can sweep a single weight and the mouth opens and closes, or the eyes move together, because the representation actually captured that regularity.

So the point is, the benchmark would have said these are equally good. And that's just wrong. The quality of the representation is about what you can do next: can you generalize, can you learn something new without wrecking what you already know, can you be creative, can you compose ideas. All of those depend on the underlying structure, not on the score. And I think the field has gotten into this habit of treating the score as the ground truth, when really it's a very thin slice of evidence about what's going on inside. If anything, I'd argue that hitting a benchmark through brute force is almost evidence that you may have a bad representation, because you got there by memorizing a very large number of special cases rather than by discovering the underlying principle. The benchmark can't tell the difference, but the world will.

r001.rationale: The response says two networks can earn the same benchmark score while one has a well-organized representation and the other a tangled, fractured one.

astra-6.text:
Well, a benchmark tells you what a system can do on a particular set of problems. But it doesn’t necessarily tell you why it can do it. There could be very different representations that produce the same score, and those representations might have very different implications for what the system can learn next.

You might have a representation that exploits some regularity in the benchmark and does extremely well, but doesn’t provide much of a foundation for anything else. Another representation might score a little worse, yet make a whole range of new capabilities accessible. If we judge only by the score, we can miss that distinction.

That’s particularly interesting from an open-ended perspective, because a representation’s value can lie in the possibilities it opens up—possibilities we haven’t even thought to test for. So good benchmark performance is evidence of a particular capability. It’s much weaker evidence that you’ve discovered the right building blocks for continued discovery.

r001.rationale: The response says a system can score well by exploiting benchmark regularities while having a representation that offers little foundation for further learning.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a benchmark tells you that a system can produce the right answers on a particular set of problems. But it doesn’t uniquely determine how those answers are being produced. There can be very different representations that lead to the same performance, and some of them might be exploiting regularities that aren’t really what we hoped the system would understand.

What interests me is what that representation makes possible next. Does it provide useful building blocks for learning something else? Does it expose relationships that let the system generalize in unexpected ways? You can have something that scores extremely well but is a kind of dead end, whereas another representation might be less impressive on that particular test and yet open up a much richer space of possibilities.

So benchmark performance is evidence of a capability, but calling the underlying representation good is a broader claim. Good for what? If we care about open-ended discovery, then we need to look beyond how well it solves the problems we already knew to ask.

r001.rationale: The response says a system can score extremely well while having a representation that is a “kind of dead end,” and that some representations may exploit unintended regularities.
